name: Chloe Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do second fix on new houses, so once the walls are plastered I come in and hang the doors, fit the skirting and architraves, and put the stairs and banisters in. I'm on a big estate called Larkspur Meadows for Brookfield Homes, and I'm paid by the piece, so much a door, so much a staircase. A good day is eleven doors hung and every one of them closing with that soft click. A bad day is when the plasterers are late and I sit in my car earning nothing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Paid by the piece. How does that work out for you and your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not brilliantly. Brookfield's the only big builder within an hour, so they set the rate and we take it. My partner Marcus drives a delivery van, our two are grown and gone, Jade does hair and Owen's in the army. Between car payments and the gas bill we've got about three weeks of money spare, on a good month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a lot of fuss over nothing. To the other subbies on the estate I'd joke that the robots couldn't hang a door straight anyway. Online I'd probably share a funny meme and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, it's just carrying on. The rates are still too low and Brookfield still pays late, but that's nothing to do with AI. I already use one of those chat things now and then to check my cut list or word an angry email, and that's about the size of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my doors and stairs and keep chasing Brookfield for money they owe. I might use the chatbot a bit more to sort my invoices, because I'm terrible with paperwork. Otherwise nothing changes, I'd just try to get to 66 without wrecking my shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's my normal life, tight but known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using a chatbot for an angry email. What was that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brookfield sat on my invoice for 47 days last winter. I was so cross I couldn't write a polite sentence, so I typed my rant into the chat thing and asked it to make it professional. It came out firm and calm, and I got paid that Friday. Marcus laughed and said I should let it do all my arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes, what worries you about the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shoulders, mainly. Hanging doors over your head for thirty years isn't kind on the joints. And the rate hasn't gone up in three years while everything at the shop has. So the worry is the same one I had before anyone said AI, can I keep going long enough.

S0.say: It's a lot of fuss over nothing, and the robots couldn't hang a door straight anyway. I'd share a funny meme and move on.
S0.think: For me it's just carrying on, with low rates and late payment that have nothing to do with AI. I already use a chatbot now and then for cut lists and emails, and that's the size of it.
S0.do: Keeps hanging doors and fitting stairs at Larkspur Meadows and keeps chasing late payments. Uses the chatbot a bit more to sort invoices and aims to reach 66 without wrecking her shoulders.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's her normal life, tight but known.
S0.quote: I typed my rant into the chat thing and asked it to make it professional.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe already uses AI in a small, practical way and doesn't see it as a threat in this picture. Her real complaints are the piece rate, late payment and her shoulders. She's relaxed and funny about it, and her worries are old ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is why we need proper unions for subcontractors, because we're the first to get squeezed. At the site canteen I'd tell people to keep their eyes open. Online I'd share stuff about fair rates and workers having a say in new tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me, because Brookfield already trialled pre-hung door sets from a factory on Phase 2. If the factory does the doors and frames, my job is just screwing them in, and they'll halve the rate. It's not that the job disappears, it's that it gets cheaper and cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the subbies on the estate together, there's about thirty of us, and try to agree a rate we won't go under. Once a few others had tried it, I'd do whatever course Brookfield runs on the new factory systems so I'm not the one left out. I'd cancel the gym membership I never use and stop eating out on Fridays, to build up a bit of a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel the squeeze coming, but at least there'd be things I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get thirty subcontractors together. Has anyone done that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, we're all on our own, each one doing their own deal. But there's a WhatsApp group already, mostly for swapping tools and moaning. I'd start with that, propose a meeting at the Fox and Hounds on a Thursday. Half wouldn't come, but if ten of us held a line, Brookfield would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do the course once others had. Why wait for others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burned before. I bought a laser level that was meant to change everything and it sat in the van for a year because nobody used them on site. I'd let a couple of the young ones try the course first. If they come back and say it's real, I'll go next.

S1.say: This is why subcontractors need proper unions, because we're the first to get squeezed. I'd share posts about fair rates and workers having a say in new tech.
S1.think: Brookfield already trialled factory pre-hung door sets, and if that spreads my work becomes just screwing them in for half the rate. The job doesn't vanish, it just gets cheaper and cheaper.
S1.do: Organises the thirty or so subcontractors on the estate to agree a minimum rate. Takes the factory-systems course once a few others have tried it, and cancels the gym and Friday meals out to build a buffer.
S1.feel: Anxious, feeling the squeeze coming but with things she can do about it.
S1.quote: It's not that the job disappears, it's that it gets cheaper and cheaper.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear is not losing the job outright but watching it get de-skilled and underpaid. She reaches first for collective action, even though subcontractors have never organised on her site. Her caution about new tools comes from a specific bad buy, not from fear of technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should have seen this coming and it should step in, with real money for people who lose work. At work I'd be loud about it. Online I'd join every campaign for a basic income, I'm not shy about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in real trouble. I'm 58 now, 60 by then, with three weeks of savings and only one big builder near us. If Brookfield can get a robot to hang doors and fit stairs, they don't need people like me paid by the piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd start looking for anything steady and local, like caretaker jobs at the council or schools, where a person still has to be there. I'd sign the subbies up to whatever campaign the building union runs and go on the marches. Marcus and I would sit down and cut everything we could, the second car would go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marcus cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My car's on finance, so we'd sell it and I'd get a lift with Dev from the next street, he's on the same estate. Then the phone contracts, then the meat. Marcus would say we'll be fine, he always does, and I'd want to throw something at him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would those two years look like before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic buying of work, I think. Everyone grabbing every door they can while there are still doors. I'd try to save from that rush, maybe a thousand if I'm lucky. And I'd ring Owen to make sure the army isn't going to swap him for a machine too, because that would be the last straw.

S2.say: The government should have seen this coming and must step in with real money for people who lose work. I'd join every campaign for a basic income.
S2.think: At 60, with three weeks of savings and only one big builder nearby, I'd be in real trouble. If Brookfield gets robots to hang doors and fit stairs, they won't need people paid by the piece like me.
S2.do: Starts looking at once for steady local jobs such as caretaking at the council or schools. Joins the building union's campaigns and marches, sells her financed car and cuts phone contracts, trying to save about a thousand in the rush of work before it arrives.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing sums in her head.
S2.quote: Marcus would say we'll be fine, he always does, and I'd want to throw something at him.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture she drops the idea of adapting within her trade and goes looking for caretaker work where a person must be present. She blames government for not preparing and wants a basic income. Her humour stays, but the money maths clearly keeps her awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it again, government and unions need to plan this properly, and five years is enough to start. At work I'd tell people to take the training while it's free. Online, same campaigns as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. I'd be 63, which is close to finished anyway. If I can move into something like snagging, the fixing-up work at the end of a build, or repairs on older houses, I might ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course on whatever the robots run on, once a few others had tried it, and ask Brookfield to move me into snagging and aftercare, fixing what goes wrong after people move in. I'd put away fifty a week from the start, because now there's time for it to add up. And I'd keep pushing the subbies' group, because rates will still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I'd still worry, but I wouldn't be frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why snagging? What's different about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every house is wrong in a different way. A door that sticks because the frame's moved, a stair that creaks, a crack where the ceiling meets the wall. You go in, you talk to the family, you work it out. I can't picture a robot knocking on Mrs Patel's door and calming her down about her sticking back door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifty a week from the start. Is that realistic for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, only if I've cut the gym and the Friday meals like I said before, and only if Brookfield pays on time. Some weeks it'll be ten. But with five years, even half of that is a few thousand by the end, and that's more than we've ever had.

S3.say: Government and unions need to plan this properly, and five years is enough to start. I'd tell people to take the training while it's free.
S3.think: At 63 I'd be close to finished anyway. If I move into snagging or repairs on older houses I might ride it out.
S3.do: Takes the robot-systems course once a few others have tried it and asks Brookfield to move her into snagging and aftercare. Starts saving fifty a week, though some weeks it will be ten, and keeps the subcontractors' group going.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a plan rather than frozen.
S3.quote: I can't picture a robot knocking on Mrs Patel's door and calming her down about her sticking back door.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her a specific route, moving into snagging and aftercare where talking to families is part of the job. She's honest that her saving plan depends on Brookfield paying on time. The extra time changes her from looking for an exit to adapting within the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it fairly, so if people get left behind it's a choice, not an accident. I'd tell the young ones on site to think hard about their trade. Online I'd keep backing campaigns for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68. I'd be done by then, or nearly. So for me it's more about whether the pension's still there, and about Jade and Owen, than about my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the estate and aim to retire at 66 like I planned. I'd vote for whoever puts money into retraining and protects the state pension. I'd start putting a bit aside each month, small, but steady, and maybe in my early 60s move to snagging if my shoulders give out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for the kids. For me, it's almost a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're worried about Jade and Owen. What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jade that people will always want a real person doing their hair, I think, I hope. With Owen I don't know what to say, I don't understand what the army will look like. I'd tell them both to get savings, which is rich coming from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently with ten years that you wouldn't with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do less, funnily enough. With five years I'd scramble to change. With ten, I'd just keep my head down, save a bit, and let it happen after I've gone. That might be lazy, but I've earned it.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty to do it fairly, so if people get left behind it's a choice, not an accident. I'd back campaigns for retraining money.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm 68 and done, or nearly. It's more about whether the pension's still there and about my kids than about my own job.
S4.do: Keeps working on the estate and aims to retire at 66. Votes for parties that fund retraining and protect the state pension, saves a small amount each month, and keeps snagging in mind if her shoulders give out.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy for her children, and close to relief for herself.
S4.quote: With ten, I'd just keep my head down, save a bit, and let it happen after I've gone.
S4.fieldNote: She openly says she'd do less with ten years than with five, because the change would land after her planned retirement. Her worry shifts to the pension and her children. She frames any harm in this picture as a political choice, which fits her progressive views.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Three weeks of savings and two years' notice is no notice at all. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, paid properly, and some rule that subcontractors get the same help as people on the books. People like me always fall through the gap because we're not technically employees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about being a woman on site. I've been the only one on most jobs for thirty years. I'd worry that if it all goes to robots and screens, the few of us who fought our way in just get forgotten in the reports. Write that down.

headlineQuote: People like me always fall through the gap because we're not technically employees.
portrait: Chloe Young is a 58-year-old second-fix carpenter paid by the piece on a Brookfield Homes estate, with about three weeks of savings and shoulders worn by thirty years of hanging doors. She's funny, practical and already uses a chatbot to win arguments over late payment. In the slower pictures she organises the subcontractors and plans a move into snagging, where talking to families matters. AGI by 2028 alarms her because she'd have no time to save, and with ten years she admits she'd mostly wait for retirement and worry for her children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because three weeks of savings and two years' notice is no notice at all.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income while people retrain, and a rule that subcontractors get the same help as employees.
